docs.title: Agential Control
docs.text: Agential control is the ability to adjust the execution of an action as the performance unfolds, representing a key component of skill development and exercise. This concept is central to understanding how AI systems may affect human capacities, as it distinguishes between skilled activity and mere habit or automatic response.

docs.title: Definition and Characteristics
docs.text:
To be skilled in something is to have agential control over it, which involves:

  1. Initiating the activity: The agent has full control over starting the task, rather than responding to environmental triggers
  2. Adjusting execution: The ability to modify performance in response to changing circumstances
  3. Flexible links between thought and action: Developing connections that continue to evolve even after expertise has been achieved

As Nancy Sherman (1991) explains, "as agency develops, the balance between automaticity and control shifts through a process of tuning and attuning."

docs.title: Contrast with Habit
docs.text:
Skills differ from habits in an important respect:

  • Skills: Require control over initiating the task; the agent has full control over starting the activity
  • Habits: Are elicited in response to environmental triggers; the agent performs the activity in response to the trigger

For example, a habitual activity is one triggered by something in the environment (like checking notifications when a phone buzzes), whereas a skilled activity is one where the agent has full control over initiating the activity (like deliberately practicing a musical instrument).

docs.title: Importance for Capacity Development
docs.text:
Agential control is crucial for developing core human capacities because:

  1. It enables self-criticism and improvement when plans fail
  2. It supports the development of practical wisdom through real-world experience
  3. It allows for creative adaptation to novel situations
  4. It preserves responsibility for outcomes, fostering growth

docs.title: AI's Impact on Agential Control
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine agential control in several ways:

  • Over-automation: When AI systems make decisions for users, they remove opportunities to practice judgment
  • Reactive interfaces: Design patterns that encourage users to respond to algorithmic suggestions rather than initiate actions
  • Personalized recommendations: Systems that anticipate user needs may reduce opportunities for independent decision-making

For instance, when users rely on artificial-personal-assistants to plan their lives, they may become "plan-followers rather than plan-formers," diminishing their capacity for practical reasoning.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text: For market research professionals, preserving agential control is essential for maintaining high-quality insights. Research tools that completely automate analysis may deprive researchers of opportunities to develop critical thinking skills. Instead, AI-augmented tools should preserve opportunities for researchers to exercise control over the analytical process.

docs.title: Ai democratization
docs.text: AI democratization refers to the process where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: AI democratization describes how artificial intelligence makes advanced capabilities accessible by automating complex expert tasks, thereby reducing expertise requirements for certain occupations. As quantified in Figure 2 of the PwC 2026 report, this process affects 52% of global job postings. Concrete examples include [[recruiters]] (AI automates CV screening while humans handle contract negotiation) and [[inventory-clerks]] (AI manages stock optimization while humans perform physical movement). Figure 3 demonstrates democratization is particularly strong in high AI exposure jobs, where expertise requirements decrease significantly. Crucially, Figure 11 reveals that despite reduced expertise demands, democratized roles maintain high epoch-score (0.48), indicating continued reliance on human capabilities for remaining tasks—often involving physical dexterity, adaptability, or interpersonal skills. The report warns that while democratization expands job accessibility (e.g., enabling non-experts to perform data analysis), it may compress career ladders and reduce skill development opportunities without targeted interventions. This concept represents one of two primary pathways (alongside ai-professionalization) in AI's labor market restructuring. Organizations can leverage democratization through the ai-job-future-framework's 'Supply and Demand' dimension, redesigning roles to balance AI efficiency with human execution. The trend is accelerating post-2022, as shown in Figure 9's widening skill transformation gap, requiring proactive workforce planning to ensure equitable access to emerging opportunities in democratized roles.

docs.title: AI Deskilling Structural Problem
docs.text: The AI deskilling structural problem refers to the phenomenon where AI systems undermine human capacities not merely through individual choices, but through systemic conditions that create environments hostile to capacity cultivation. This concept, developed by Avigail Ferdman (2026), moves beyond framing deskilling as an individual responsibility issue to recognize its structural dimensions.

docs.title: Core Argument
docs.text:
The central thesis is that:

"AI's influence creates systemic conditions that could inhibit the development and exercise of human capacities by undermining the process of capacity cultivation."

This perspective challenges the notion that individuals can simply "will themselves" to resist deskilling, recognizing that socio-technical environments play a crucial role in shaping human capacities.

docs.title: 1. Capacity Impoverishment
docs.text:
• Definition: Inadequate development of core human capacities leading to diminished human flourishing
  • Core capacities affected: Epistemic, social, moral, creative, and volitional capacities
  • Consequence: "Capacity-deskilling is bad because inadequate development of these capacities can lead to 'capacity impoverishment,' which, in turn, diminishes us as humans and undermines our flourishing."

docs.title: 2. Structural Dimensions
docs.text:
• Affordance fields: Environments that restrict action possibilities for capacity development
  • Embodiment: Digital interfaces that undermine physical presence necessary for certain capacities
  • Intersubjectivity: Systems that replace human mentoring relationships
  • Habituation process: AI that shortcuts the gradual development of skills

docs.title: 3. Capacity-Hostile vs. Conducive Environments
docs.text:
• Hostile environments: Restrict, limit, or create narrow fields of affordances for capacity development
  • Conducive environments: Encourage the cultivation and exercise of human capacities

docs.title: Evidence of Deskilling
docs.text:
Growing evidence shows AI dependence leads to:

  • Erosion of critical thinking (Bonicalzi et al. 2023; Gerlich 2025; Lee et al. 2025)
  • Decline in decision-making and analytical reasoning (Zhai et al. 2024)
  • Reduced activity awareness and competence maintenance (Rinta-Kahila et al. 2023)
  • Diminished diagnostic reasoning and clinical judgment in healthcare (NHS England 2023)

docs.title: Why Individual Responsibility Isn't Enough
docs.text:
The structural perspective argues that expecting individuals to resist deskilling overlooks:

  1. Environmental determinants: We develop capacities in response to our social and material environment
  2. Shared valuing: Learning to value capacities requires intersubjective contexts
  3. Embodied interaction: Certain capacities can only develop through physical presence
  4. Systemic design: Technology affordances make certain behaviors more likely regardless of individual dispositions

As Ferdman explains, "the context in which a user's behavior occurs can better explain the behavior than appealing to the user's dispositions."

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research professionals, the structural deskilling problem has several important implications:

  • Research design: Understanding how AI-augmented tools might affect researchers' capacity development
  • Consumer behavior: Recognizing how AI-mediated environments shape decision-making capacities
  • Ethical considerations: Evaluating whether research tools create capacity-conducive or hostile environments
  • Long-term impacts: Considering how AI adoption might change the skill sets required in the industry

docs.title: Related Concepts
docs.text: See capacity-hostile-environments, habituation-process, and agential-control for related frameworks analyzing how AI affects human capacities.

  • Vallor, S. (2015). Technology and the Virtues: A Philosophical Guide to a Future Worth Wanting. Oxford University Press.
  • Mitcham, C. (2024). Virtuous Superheroes: The Limits of Individual Responsibility in the Age of AI.

docs.title: Ai job future framework
docs.text: A framework of four questions to analyze how AI is reshaping specific occupations, developed by PwC in their 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The AI Job Future Framework, introduced in Figure 6 of PwC's 2026 report, provides a structured methodology to assess AI's occupational impact through four critical questions: (1) Expertise: How is AI changing required human expertise? (e.g., democratization reduces expertise needs while professionalization increases them); (2) Supply and Demand: How might job demand and worker supply shift as AI reshapes roles?; (3) AI's limitations: Where is human oversight needed for quality control or atypical cases?; and (4) Environmental forces: How do regulations, business bottlenecks, or ethics constrain AI adoption? The report demonstrates the framework's application across diverse occupations: For [[pharmacists]], AI handles prescription processing (Expertise shift) but humans manage patient counseling (AI's limitations); for [[software-developers]], AI generates code but humans focus on architecture (Environmental forces). Figure 9 validates the framework by showing how high AI exposure roles undergo 2.2x faster skill changes, directly addressing the Supply and Demand dimension. Organizations using this tool can anticipate skill shifts, redesign roles, and develop targeted training—particularly valuable for navigating the 'superstar effect' (Figure 12). The framework also explains wage dynamics: roles requiring human oversight of AI (Question 3) command higher premiums, as seen in Figure 15's 62% average AI skill premium. By systematically addressing these questions, employers can transform AI disruption into opportunity, while workers identify future-proof career paths in the evolving labor market. This methodology has become essential for strategic workforce planning in the AI era.

AI professionalization refers to the process where AI automates less expert tasks, leaving more expert tasks for humans. This phenomenon represents one pathway through which AI reshapes occupations, increasing the premium on specialized human expertise.

docs.title: New Evidence and Refinement
docs.text:
The mrii-2026-market-research-study provides compelling evidence of AI professionalization in the insights industry: - As AI handles routine analytical tasks, value is shifting upstream toward strategic functions - Insights teams must evolve from delivering answers to shaping decisions, driving growth, and influencing strategy - Pam Forbus of [[mondelez]] states: "AI will increasingly answer questions, deliver insights, execute projects, and support stakeholders faster and at lower cost than ever before. That doesn't diminish the role of insights teams; it fundamentally changes it."

This represents a specific manifestation of professionalization where AI automation of basic tasks elevates the importance of strategic human capabilities.

The value-chain-shift concept further explains this dynamic - as AI makes answers faster and cheaper, the answers themselves become less differentiated, pushing value creation toward higher-order strategic functions.

docs.title: Relationship to Skills Development
docs.text:
A critical finding from the MRII study reveals a professionalization paradox: - Professionals prioritize learning technical AI skills - Leaders value business acumen, communication, and strategic influence more highly

This disconnect threatens to undermine the professionalization process, as organizations may automate tasks without adequately developing the human capabilities needed for the elevated roles.

docs.title: Connection to Entry-Level Dynamics
docs.text: The burning-glass-beyond-binary report shows that professionalization occurs alongside automation within the same occupations. This creates particular challenges for entry-level positions through the entry-level-squeeze, as foundational tasks that build expertise are automated before new developmental pathways are established.

docs.title: Organizational Implications
docs.text: Successful navigation of AI professionalization requires: - Redesigning roles to preserve meaningful human involvement in value-creating activities - Developing new apprenticeship models that build expertise despite automated foundational tasks - Aligning skill development priorities with the evolving value chain

docs.title: Capacity-Conducive Environments
docs.text: Capacity-conducive environments are socio-technical contexts that actively encourage the development and exercise of core human capacities. This concept, developed in contrast to capacity-hostile-environments, provides a normative framework for designing AI systems that support rather than undermine human flourishing.

docs.title: Definition and Characteristics
docs.text:
A capacity-conducive environment:

  1. Expands action possibilities: Provides rich opportunities to engage in activities requiring competent exercise of human capacities
  2. Supports deep skilling: Affords pathways for well-rounded development and mastery of capacities
  3. Facilitates habituation: Creates conditions for the gradual, intersubjective process of becoming skilled
  4. Encourages shared valuing: Provides contexts where the value of capacities is collectively recognized and reinforced

These environments recognize that the proper cultivation of core capacities depends on inhabiting spaces that afford sufficient invitations for valuable activities.

docs.title: Key Components
docs.text:
Three essential elements characterize capacity-conducive environments:

  1. Embodied engagement: Spaces that encourage physical presence and interaction, recognizing that "being embodied is critical for becoming skilled" in social and moral capacities
  2. Intersubjective learning: Contexts that support mentor-mentee relationships and shared understanding of both the product of skilled activity and the skill itself
  3. Volitional encouragement: Environments that invite users to exercise their capacity to will, rather than making decisions for them

docs.title: Examples in Practice
docs.text:
Effective capacity-conducive environments include:

  • Community centers and public spaces: That encourage structured and unstructured embodied interactions
  • Public libraries: That afford opportunities for reading while also providing social contexts for discussing ideas
  • AI-augmented professional tools: That preserve opportunities for practitioners to develop expertise while benefiting from automation of routine tasks

docs.title: Design Principles for AI Systems
docs.text:
When designing AI systems, capacity-conducive approaches would:

  • Preserve opportunities for users to exercise agential control
  • Create space for habituation through graduated challenges
  • Support intersubjective learning rather than replacing human mentors
  • Encourage embodied interaction where appropriate
  • Avoid creating "affordance shrinkage" that systematically reduces action possibilities

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research professionals, capacity-conducive environments are essential for maintaining high-quality insights. Research tools that preserve opportunities for researchers to develop critical thinking and analytical skills will ultimately produce more valuable insights than those that completely automate the research process.

Additionally, understanding how consumer environments affect capacity development can inform more nuanced interpretations of consumer behavior and decision-making.

docs.title: Capacity-Hostile Environments
docs.text: Capacity-hostile environments are socio-technical contexts that restrict, limit, or create a narrow field of affordances for the development and exercise of core human capacities. This concept, introduced in Ferdman's 2026 paper "AI Deskilling is a Structural Problem," provides a framework for evaluating how AI systems may undermine human flourishing.

docs.title: Definition and Characteristics
docs.text:
A capacity-hostile environment:

  1. Restricts action possibilities: Limits opportunities to engage in activities requiring competent exercise of human capacities
  2. Encourages shallow skilling: Affords opportunities for only superficial development of capacities
  3. Undermines habituation: Disrupts the gradual process of becoming skilled through practice
  4. Discourages shared valuing: Fails to provide intersubjective contexts where the value of capacities is collectively recognized

These environments are particularly problematic when they lead to "affordance shrinkage" - a systematic, enduring reduction in action possibilities that discourages users from finding compensatory pathways.

docs.title: Examples in AI Contexts
docs.text:
Several AI applications create capacity-hostile environments:

  • Over-automated workflows: When AI systems replace routine tasks without providing opportunities for users to practice judgment, they deprive users of "the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature" (Lee et al. 2025)
  • Disembodied interactions: Environments that lack physical presence make it harder to form meaningful relationships and develop moral capacities
  • Algorithmic decision-making: Systems that offload moral reasoning to non-human agents undermine the development of practical wisdom

docs.title: Contrast with Capacity-Conducive Environments
docs.text:
Capacity-hostile environments stand in contrast to capacity-conducive-environments, which actively encourage the development and exercise of human capacities through:

  • Rich opportunities for embodied interaction
  • Intersubjective contexts for shared valuing
  • Gradual challenges that support habituation
  • Affordances that encourage exercising the capacity to will

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research professionals, recognizing capacity-hostile environments is crucial when designing AI-augmented research tools. Systems that automate data collection or analysis without preserving opportunities for researchers to develop critical thinking skills could ultimately undermine the quality of insights produced.

The concept also has implications for understanding how AI affects consumer behavior and decision-making - environments that are hostile to capacity development may produce less thoughtful consumer responses.

docs.title: Embodiment in Skilling
docs.text: Embodiment in skilling refers to the essential role of physical presence and sensory experience in the development of human capacities. This concept explains why disembodied AI interactions may undermine the cultivation of certain skills, particularly social and moral capacities.

docs.title: Definition and Characteristics
docs.text:
Embodiment in the context of skill development involves:

  1. Physical presence: Being situated in space with others through voice, gaze, and bodily cues
  2. Participatory sense-making: Co-creating meaning through embodied interaction
  3. Spontaneous recognition: Naturally perceiving others as moral agents through embodied cues
  4. Shared history: Creating common experiences through physical co-presence

According to the Enactive Approach in cognition, "embodied 'participatory sense-making' is constitutive of social cognition," meaning that physical interaction itself is part of the cognitive process that unfolds between participants.

docs.title: Importance for Capacity Development
docs.text: Embodiment is critical for developing several core capacities:

docs.title: Social and Moral Capacities
docs.text:
• Moral attention: Requires perceiving others as embodied beings similar to ourselves
  • Friendship: Disembodied interactions make it harder to form meaningful relationships
  • Empathy: Physical presence enhances the ability to understand others' emotional states

As Ferdman (2026) explains, "without being embodied in a social interaction—without the return of the gaze of the other—we would be hard-pressed to recognize them spontaneously as moral agents."

docs.title: Epistemic Capacities
docs.text:
• Learning from others: Physical presence enhances knowledge transfer
  • Practical wisdom: Developed through real-world embodied experiences
  • Critical thinking: Enhanced through face-to-face dialogue and debate

docs.title: AI's Impact on Embodiment
docs.text:
AI systems often create disembodied environments that undermine capacity development:

  • Digital interfaces: Replace physical presence with screens and text
  • Algorithmic mediation: Filter and shape interactions in ways that reduce embodied connection
  • Automation bias: Encourages users to trust AI outputs over embodied human judgment

For example, when users rely on artificial-personal-assistants for life planning, they miss opportunities to develop practical wisdom through embodied interactions with mentors and peers.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research professionals, embodiment has several important implications:

  • Research methods: In-person interviews and focus groups provide richer data than purely digital methods
  • Team collaboration: Physical co-working spaces support better knowledge sharing than fully remote arrangements
  • Consumer behavior: Understanding how digital environments affect decision-making capacities
  • Tool design: Creating research tools that preserve opportunities for embodied interaction

docs.text: See habituation-process, intersubjectivity-in-skilling, and capacity-hostile-environments for related frameworks.

  • Di Paolo, E., & Thompson, E. (2014). The enactive approach. In L. Shapiro (Ed.), The Routledge Handbook of Embodied Cognition (pp. 68-78). Routledge.

docs.title: Entry level squeeze
docs.text: The entry-level squeeze describes the growing pressure on traditional entry-level positions in knowledge work as AI capabilities automate foundational tasks that historically served as training grounds for developing professional expertise.

docs.title: Capacity Development Challenges for Entry-Level Workers
docs.text: While recent evidence shows entry-level headcount is growing among high-intensity AI adopters, the nature of entry-level work is changing in ways that may affect capacity development for junior professionals.

docs.title: Deskilling Risks in Entry-Level Roles
docs.text:
The ai-deskilling-structural-problem framework reveals several risks for entry-level workers:

  • Reduced habituation opportunities: When AI automates routine tasks, entry-level workers lose "the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature" (Lee et al. 2025)
  • Shallow skill development: Entry into professions may become more superficial without proper mentoring
  • Disembodied learning: Digital workflows may limit embodied interaction necessary for social capacity development
  • Affordance shrinkage: Systematic reduction in action possibilities for developing practical wisdom

docs.title: Structural Dimensions
docs.text:
These challenges are not merely individual responsibility issues but stem from structural conditions:

"We develop and exercise our epistemic, moral, social, and creative capacities in response to our social and material environment" (Ferdman 2026). When entry-level environments become [[capacity-hostile]], junior professionals may struggle to develop the "arts of personhood" required for long-term success.

docs.title: Evidence from Research
docs.text: Studies show that young people growing up with digital tools already struggle with "everyday but essential" skills like empathy, time management, speaking to others, problem-solving and critical thinking (Halliday 2025). AI tools like artificial-personal-assistants could potentially exacerbate this deskilling.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these findings suggest:

  • Entry-level training programs must intentionally preserve opportunities for capacity development
  • Mentorship relationships are crucial for counteracting AI-mediated deskilling
  • Workflows should balance AI augmentation with human skill development
  • Organizations should design capacity-conducive environments for junior staff

The structural perspective emphasizes that "we cannot expect agents to be what Mitcham (2024) calls 'virtuous superheroes' and properly cultivate their human capacities if their social environment does not value the full maturation of these capacities."

See capacity-conducive-environments and habituation-process for related frameworks addressing these challenges.

docs.title: Habituation Process
docs.text: The habituation process is the gradual, slow development of skill through practice and experience. This concept is central to understanding how human capacities are cultivated and why AI systems that shortcut this process may undermine human flourishing.

docs.title: Definition and Characteristics
docs.text:
Habituation involves:

  1. Gradual progression: Moving through stages of skill development from novice to expert
  2. Concrete experience: Learning through specific cases rather than abstract principles
  3. Refinement through trial: Improving through successive attempts and learning from mistakes
  4. Inculcation: Internalizing skills through continued attunement to demands of individual cases

As Dreyfus and Dreyfus (1986) characterize it, the process comprises five stages: novice, advanced beginner, competent, proficient, and expert. Rule-following dominates early stages, while later stages are characterized by rapid, fluid, involved engagement.

docs.title: Two Essential Components
docs.text: The habituation process has two critical dimensions:

docs.title: 1. Intersubjectivity
docs.text:
• Mentor-mentee relationships: Skilled development typically requires guidance from someone more experienced
  • Shared understanding: Both mentor and mentee develop "shared valuing" of the skill
  • Social practices: Groups or societies provide mentoring environments through family, colleagues, and citizens

As Alasdair MacIntyre noted, "becoming the kind of agent who is responsive to whatever it is that skillful action requires... has to be learned from teachers and exemplars who know how to communicate this kind of responsiveness to others through the habits of a common life."

docs.title: 2. Embodiment
docs.text:
• Participatory sense-making: Embodied interaction is constitutive of social cognition
  • Recognizing others: The spontaneity of recognizing others as moral agents is inherent in embodied interaction
  • Shared history: Creating shared experiences through doing something together

Without embodiment in social interaction, it becomes much harder to form meaningful relationships and develop moral capacities.

docs.title: AI's Impact on Habituation
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine the habituation process by:

  • Automating routine tasks: Depriving users of "routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature" (Lee et al. 2025)
  • Providing instant answers: Short-circuiting the learning process that comes from struggling with problems
  • Reducing embodied interaction: Limiting opportunities for physical presence in skill development
  • Creating dependency: Encouraging users to rely on AI rather than developing their own capacities

For example, when users become overly dependent on artificial-personal-assistants for life planning, they miss opportunities to develop practical wisdom through real-world experience.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research professionals, understanding the habituation process is crucial for:

  • Designing research tools that preserve opportunities for skill development
  • Recognizing how AI-augmented tools might affect researchers' capacity development
  • Understanding how consumer environments affect decision-making capacities
  • Developing training programs that support proper habituation of research skills

docs.title: Human operating model gap
docs.text: The human operating model gap refers to the growing disparity between the rapid advancement of AI capabilities and the slower adaptation of human systems, processes, and skills required to leverage AI effectively within organizations.

docs.title: Workforce Composition Changes with AI Adoption
docs.text: Recent evidence reveals how AI adoption is reshaping workforce composition across roles, highlighting the growing gap between rapidly advancing AI capabilities and slower human system adaptation.

docs.title: Role-Specific Employment Effects
docs.text:
The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study provides detailed evidence of how AI adoption affects different job functions:

  • Broad-based growth: High-intensity adopters showed growth across multiple roles:
  • Sales headcount: +10.3%
  • Administrative headcount: +7.8%
  • Engineering headcount: +7.3%
  • Customer service headcount: +6.3%

  • Scientist headcount: +5.6%

  • Entry-level expansion: Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% among high-intensity adopters

  • Managerial shifts: Manager-plus share fell by 1.52 percentage points despite overall growth

docs.title: Structural Workforce Shifts
docs.text:
These findings reveal several important patterns:

  1. Non-binary impact: AI adoption doesn't simply eliminate jobs but reshapes workforce composition
  2. Intensity matters: Only high-intensity adopters (top tercile of AI spend) showed significant growth
  3. Gradual emergence: Gains followed a learning curve, emerging 6-12 months after adoption
  4. Sector concentration: Effects were strongest in the Information sector

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these workforce shifts suggest:

  • AI is currently augmenting rather than replacing human capabilities in information work
  • Strategic AI investment may support growth across multiple functions
  • Entry-level positions may expand as firms scale with AI assistance
  • Workforce planning must account for the gradual nature of AI integration

The study notes that "the earliest signs of growth emerge roughly 6-12 months after adoption, perhaps after firms establish best practices, integrate AI tools into workflows, and are subsequently able to make new investments and hire staff."

docs.title: Bridging the Gap
docs.text:
To address the human operating model gap, market research firms should:

  • Develop AI adoption strategies that align with workforce development
  • Create pathways for employees to develop AI-augmented capabilities
  • Recognize that successful integration requires time for habituation
  • Design capacity-conducive environments that preserve opportunities for skill development

See value-chain-shift and ai-professionalization for related frameworks analyzing AI's impact on organizational structures.

docs.title: Intersubjectivity in Skilling
docs.text: Intersubjectivity in skilling refers to the shared understanding dimension of skill development, where learning occurs through relationships with others who guide, model, and share the value of the skill. This concept is essential for understanding why AI systems that replace human interaction may undermine capacity development.

docs.title: Definition and Characteristics
docs.text:
Intersubjectivity in the context of skill development involves:

  1. Shared valuing: Both mentor and mentee come to view the value of the skill as their own
  2. Guided practice: A mentor provides appropriate challenges and feedback at each stage of development
  3. Social practices: Groups or societies create environments that generate reasons for action
  4. Constitutive aims: Activities have telos that ultimately help people fare well rather than badly

As Kate Manne argues, "social practices are often what generates moral reasons for action, as they have a constitutive aim or telos, which is ultimately the aim of helping people fare well rather than badly."

docs.title: 1. Mentor-Mentee Relationship
docs.text:
• Guidance: A good mentor is typically necessary to cultivate the proper motivational structure
  • Value transmission: Mentors instill not only mechanical aspects of the skill but also its value
  • Shared intentions: Both mentor and mentee develop aligned goals for skill development

This relationship is crucial because "learning to value a capacity is part of the process of its habituation." Without proper mentoring, learners cannot develop deep appreciation for the skill.

docs.title: 2. Societal Scale
docs.text:
• Social practices: The family, colleagues, citizens, and other social groups provide mentoring environments
  • Shared norms: Societies establish expectations about what constitutes skilled performance
  • Collective understanding: Communities develop shared interpretations of what the skill means

Alasdair MacIntyre noted that "learning is carried out through the practices of the common life," emphasizing how social context shapes skill development.

docs.title: AI's Impact on Intersubjectivity
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine intersubjectivity in several ways:

  • Replacing human mentors: When AI provides guidance without human connection
  • Lacking shared valuing: AI cannot genuinely share the value of a skill with users
  • Reducing embodied interaction: Digital interfaces limit the richness of mentor-mentee relationships
  • Creating isolated learning: Users develop skills without connection to social practices

For instance, when users rely on artificial-personal-assistants for life planning advice, they miss opportunities to develop shared understanding about values and goals through human relationships.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research professionals, understanding intersubjectivity is crucial for:

  • Designing research tools that preserve opportunities for collaborative learning
  • Recognizing how AI-augmented tools might affect team dynamics and knowledge sharing
  • Understanding how consumer decision-making is shaped by social contexts
  • Developing training programs that maintain human connection in skill development

docs.title: Related Concepts
docs.text: See habituation-process, embodiment-in-skilling, and capacity-conducive-environments for related frameworks.

docs.text:

  • MacIntyre, A. (2017). Ethics in the Conflicts of Modernity: An Essay on Desire, Practical Reasoning, and Narrative. Cambridge University Press.
  • Ferdman, A. (2026). AI deskilling is a structural problem. AI & Society, 41, 3001-3013.

docs.title: Seniorised roles
docs.text: The phenomenon where entry-level roles increasingly demand skills traditionally required in senior positions due to AI adoption.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: Seniorised roles describe the accelerating trend where entry-level positions now require skills traditionally associated with senior roles, driven by AI automation of foundational tasks. Figure 8 in the PwC 2026 report provides compelling evidence: in the US top AI exposure quartile, seniorised entry-level job postings are projected to grow 35% between 2019-2025, while non-seniorised roles decline by 10%. This occurs because AI tools handle routine onboarding tasks (e.g., data entry for [[inventory-clerks]] or basic analysis for [[recruiters]]), compressing career ladders and elevating entry requirements. Common senior skills now appearing in entry-level descriptions include strategic decision-making frameworks, cross-departmental collaboration, client advisory capabilities, and complex problem-solving—particularly in high-growth professionalised-jobs. Figure 7 contextualizes this within broader market trends, showing high AI exposure quartile entry-level postings have flatlined since 2022, suggesting seniorisation may be a prerequisite for growth in AI-impacted roles. The report warns this trend could exacerbate early-career inequality if not balanced with structured mentorship, as new graduates face higher barriers without prior exposure to advanced skills. However, organizations using the ai-job-future-framework can mitigate risks by designing onboarding that combines AI tools with human skill development. The phenomenon represents a key manifestation of AI's impact on career progression, with implications for education systems needing to prepare students for accelerated responsibility in the AI era.

docs.title: Superstar effect
docs.text: The top 20% of most AI-exposed companies, referred to as 'superstars', achieve a significantly higher productivity growth rate.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The 'superstar effect' identifies a critical divergence among AI adopters: the top 20% of most AI-exposed firms achieve dramatically higher productivity gains than peers. This effect was documented by pwc using orbis company financial data. As revealed in Figure 12 of the PwC 2026 report, these 'superstar' companies attained 163% average productivity growth in 2025—5 times higher than the 33.5% growth rate of most AI-exposed companies as a whole. This advantage has widened steadily since 2022, with superstars accelerating their lead while other AI-exposed firms maintain moderate growth. Figure 13 shows this productivity advantage translates to headcount growth, with superstar firms expanding employment 52.2% by 2025 versus 35.7% for least exposed quartiles. Crucially, Figure 14 demonstrates these gains are shared with workers through higher wage growth (24.4% vs 16.6% in 2025). The report attributes superstar status to three factors: strategic AI integration beyond automation (leveraging the ai-job-future-framework), investment in complementary human skills, and organizational agility in addressing [[ai's limitations]]. This creates a 'winner-takes-most' dynamic where superstars capture disproportionate value—evident in Figure 16's AI specialist hiring surge within these firms. The effect has profound implications: companies failing to achieve superstar status risk falling behind in the AI transformation, while workers in superstar firms gain through both wages and career opportunities in high-growth professionalised-jobs. Policymakers must address resulting market concentration through targeted support for mid-tier AI adopters.

docs.title: Value chain shift
docs.text: The value chain shift refers to the fundamental repositioning of where value is created within market research and insights organizations as AI capabilities advance.

docs.title: Sectoral Variations in AI Impact
docs.text: Recent research reveals that AI's impact on the value chain is unevenly distributed across sectors, with significant implications for how value is created within market research organizations.

docs.title: Sectoral Employment Effects
docs.text:
The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study found that employment gains from AI adoption are concentrated in the Information sector:

  • Information sector: 13.4% headcount growth among high-intensity AI adopters
  • Professional and technical services: Positive but non-significant growth
  • All other sectors: Near-zero or imprecise effects

This pattern reflects the current state of AI adoption, which is "uniquely concentrated in Information" where "the most commercially mature AI gains appear clearest in coding-agent and software-engineering workflows."

docs.title: Implications for Market Research Value Chain
docs.text:
For market research firms, this sectoral variation suggests:

  1. Front-end transformation: Research design and data collection may see earlier AI integration
  2. Back-end resilience: Interpretation and strategic recommendation may remain more human-intensive
  3. Specialization opportunities: Firms focusing on information-intensive research may adopt AI more rapidly
  4. Competitive differentiation: Early AI adopters in research may gain productivity advantages

The study notes that "it is still early in the AI adoption curve" and "AI use cases may diffuse more slowly outside software and media." This suggests market research firms should anticipate a gradual shift in where value is created, rather than an immediate transformation.

docs.title: Strategic Considerations
docs.text:
Market research organizations should consider:

  • Where their work aligns with sectors experiencing the strongest AI impacts
  • How to position themselves to benefit from productivity gains in information processing
  • When to invest in high-intensity AI adoption versus more limited applications
  • How to develop workforce strategies that align with sector-specific AI adoption patterns

See human-operating-model-gap and ai-professionalization for related frameworks analyzing AI's impact on organizational value chains.

docs.title: Artificial Personal Assistants
docs.text: Artificial Personal Assistants (APAs) are AI systems, typically based on Large Language Models (LLMs), designed to assist with personal organization, life planning, and decision-making. Examples include AI applications built on platforms like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini that function as "always-on sounding boards" for users.

docs.title: Definition and Capabilities
docs.text:
APAs are characterized by their ability to:

  1. Adapt to individual needs: Tailor advice based on user responses, habits, and preferences
  2. Provide constant availability: Function as "an always-on sounding board with whatever subject-matter expertise you need"
  3. Offer non-judgmental listening: Provide a space for users to explore ideas without social pressure
  4. Support life planning: Help users organize their lives, find purpose, and develop self-awareness

As described by Samuel (2025), APAs function as "virtual experts in different areas, working together to create almost anything we can imagine," configured with the user's preferred tone of interaction.

docs.title: Common Use Cases
docs.text:
Research shows the most common uses of APAs include:

  • Life-planning: Organizing daily life, setting goals, and developing routines
  • Finding purpose: Exploring values and long-term direction
  • Social validation: Seeking confirmation of ideas and decisions
  • Self-regulation: Managing habits and maintaining focus
  • Interpersonal guidance: Navigating relationship challenges

A 2025 study found that users rely on APAs to "help them be more aware of their intentions, determine and define their values, get past roadblocks, and take steps to self-develop."

docs.title: Capacity-Hostile Potential
docs.text:
While APAs offer convenience, they risk creating capacity-hostile-environments by:

  1. Undermining agential control: Encouraging users to become "plan-followers rather than plan-formers"
  2. Short-circuiting habituation: Replacing the gradual process of developing practical wisdom
  3. Reducing intersubjectivity: Diminishing opportunities for shared valuing with human mentors
  4. Promoting disembodiment: Limiting embodied interactions necessary for social capacity development

For example, when users ask APAs to "help me plan my day" or "how should I fill an unscheduled hour," they miss opportunities to develop decision-making skills through small-scale choices that build toward broader life planning capabilities.

docs.title: Structural Concerns
docs.text:
The structural dimension of APA use is particularly concerning because:

  • Scale and integration: APAs are "trained to do everything for everyone," making them all-encompassing agents
  • Convenience bias: Their constant availability makes it easy to rely on them excessively
  • Lack of training wheels: Unlike human mentors, APAs don't know "when to remove itself as the training wheels"
  • Affordance shrinkage: Systematically reducing opportunities for users to develop planning capacities

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research professionals, understanding APAs is important for:

  • Recognizing how AI tools affect consumer decision-making processes
  • Designing research tools that avoid creating capacity-hostile environments
  • Understanding changing patterns of human-AI interaction in daily life
  • Developing methodologies that account for AI-mediated consumer behavior

docs.title: Lightcast
docs.text: Lightcast (formerly Emsi Burning Glass) is a labor market analytics company that provides detailed data on job postings, skills demand, and workforce trends. The company aggregates and analyzes millions of job postings from across the internet to create comprehensive labor market intelligence.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: Lightcast data serves as a primary source for PwC's Global AI Jobs Barometer analysis. According to the 2026 report, the analysis examined over one billion online job advertisements across six continents, with Lightcast providing the underlying job posting data.

docs.title: Data Collection Methodology
docs.text:
Lightcast gathers job posting data through:

  • Web scraping of major job boards and company career sites
  • Partnerships with job posting aggregators
  • Direct feeds from some large employers
  • Historical archives dating back to 2012 for certain markets

The company processes this raw data to extract structured information about required skills, qualifications, compensation, and other job characteristics.

docs.title: Application in PwC's Research
docs.text:
In the PwC 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer, Lightcast data was used to:

  • Track changes in job posting volumes across different AI exposure levels
  • Analyze skill requirements and how they evolve over time
  • Calculate wage premiums for AI-related skills
  • Identify trends in entry-level hiring patterns
  • Measure growth in AI specialist positions

docs.title: Key Insights Enabled by Lightcast Data
docs.text:
Analysis of Lightcast data revealed several critical patterns:

  • AI specialist job postings grew eight times faster than total job postings from 2012-2025
  • Entry-level job postings in the highest AI exposure quartile flatlined after 2022
  • Skills needed for the most AI-exposed jobs are changing 2.2x faster than for the least exposed jobs
  • Wage premiums for AI skills reached 62% across all sectors in 2025

docs.title: Limitations and Considerations
docs.text:
While valuable, Lightcast data has certain limitations:

  • Primarily captures formal, online job postings (may miss informal hiring)
  • Coverage varies by country and time period
  • Skill extraction relies on natural language processing of job descriptions
  • May not fully capture internal mobility or promotions

Researchers using Lightcast data, like PwC, typically note these limitations and adjust their methodologies accordingly.

See also: pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer, pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index

docs.title: ORBIS
docs.text: ORBIS is a comprehensive global business information database maintained by Bureau van Dijk (a Moody's Analytics company). It provides detailed financial, ownership, and operational data on millions of companies worldwide, serving as a critical resource for business intelligence and economic research.

docs.title: Role in AI Research
docs.text: In PwC's 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer, ORBIS data served as the primary source for company-level analysis, particularly regarding productivity, headcount, and wage growth metrics across different levels of AI exposure.

docs.title: Data Coverage
docs.text:
ORBIS includes information on:

  • Over 400 million companies globally
  • Financial statements and performance metrics
  • Ownership structures and corporate hierarchies
  • Industry classifications using standard systems like NAICS
  • Employment data and executive information

For the PwC analysis, the database provided longitudinal data from 2018-2025 for companies with consistent reporting.

docs.title: Application in PwC's Research
docs.text:
PwC used ORBIS data to:

  • Measure productivity growth (revenue per employee) across AI exposure levels
  • Track headcount changes at companies in different AI exposure quartiles
  • Analyze wage growth patterns relative to AI adoption
  • Identify the "superstar effect" among highly AI-exposed companies

docs.title: Key Insights Enabled by ORBIS Data
docs.text:
Analysis of ORBIS data revealed several critical patterns:

  • The most AI-exposed companies showed 33.5% productivity growth (2018-2025) compared to 18.7% for least exposed
  • Headcount growth at most AI-exposed companies reached 52.2% versus 23.3% for least exposed
  • Wage growth at most AI-exposed companies reached 24.4% versus 5.6% for least exposed
  • The top 20% of most AI-exposed companies ("superstars") achieved 163% productivity growth

docs.title: Methodological Considerations
docs.text:
PwC's analysis using ORBIS data included several important methodological notes:

  • Focus on larger formal firms with annual turnover of at least $50m USD
  • Exclusion of companies that exited the market during the period (creating survivorship bias)
  • Potential bias toward larger, more formalized companies in some countries
  • Company AI exposure determined by NAICS sector classification

These considerations mean the analysis reflects patterns among established businesses rather than the entire economy, but still provides valuable insights into how AI adoption correlates with business performance.

See also: pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer, superstar-effect

docs.title: PwC
docs.text: PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) is a multinational professional services network and one of the Big Four accounting firms. It provides audit and assurance, tax, and advisory services to corporations, governments, and non-profit organizations globally. With operations in 157 countries and over 360,000 employees, PwC serves as a leading authority on economic and labor market trends.

docs.title: Relevance to AI and Market Research
docs.text: PwC has emerged as a pivotal publisher of research on artificial intelligence's impact on the global labor market. Its annual Global AI Jobs Barometer report analyzes trends using data from over one billion job advertisements, providing critical insights for the market research industry. The firm's proprietary pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index methodology has become a standard for measuring AI's workforce impact.

docs.title: Key Contributions
docs.text:
• Developed the epoch-score framework for measuring human capability reliance in occupations
  • Identified the dual trends of ai-democratization (52% of jobs) and ai-professionalization (22% of jobs)
  • Documented the superstar-effect where top AI-adopting companies achieve disproportionate productivity gains
  • Quantified wage premiums for ai-skills across economic sectors

PwC's research directly informs talent strategy for market research firms navigating AI adoption. Their data provides empirical validation for skills gap analyses and workforce planning.

docs.title: Ramp
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-07-03

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Ramp is a financial operations platform that processes corporate card and bill pay transactions, providing detailed line-item spending data used to identify AI vendor payments in workforce studies. Founded to streamline corporate spending, Ramp has evolved into a critical data source for measuring actual AI adoption through financial transaction records.

docs.title: Key Products and Capabilities
docs.text:
• Corporate Card Platform: Processes payments with detailed merchant categorization
  • Bill Pay System: Tracks vendor payments beyond card transactions
  • AI Index: Proprietary classification system (Kharazian, 2026) identifying AI spend from line items
  • Spend Analytics: Provides granular insights into technology adoption patterns

docs.title: AI Index Methodology
docs.text: Ramp's AI Index identifies AI spending through: 1. Vendor Classification: Mapping merchants to AI categories (LLMs, GPU cloud, coding agents, etc.) 2. Line-Item Analysis: Text analysis of transaction details for AI-related keywords 3. Adoption Threshold: Defined as ≥$100/month for three consecutive months 4. Intensity Measurement: PEPM (AI spend per employee) over first three adoption months

docs.title: Research Applications
docs.text: Ramp's data has enabled: - First direct measurement of firm-level AI adoption intensity - Identification of high vs. low intensity adopter patterns - Sectoral analysis of AI investment concentrations - Temporal tracking of adoption waves across industries

docs.title: Key Findings from Ramp Data
docs.text:
• AI adoption highly selected: larger, more technical, faster-growing firms adopt first
  • Information sector leads adoption at 53.7% (vs. 11.5% in Accommodation/Food)
  • Small firms adopt less frequently but show higher intensity when they do adopt
  • Adoption intensity predicts employment outcomes better than binary adoption measures

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Sample skews toward tech-forward firms and knowledge work
  • May underestimate adoption in organizations using free AI tools
  • Limited visibility into internal AI development costs
  • Corporate card usage varies by firm size and industry

docs.title: Relevance to Market Research
docs.text: Ramp's methodology offers market researchers: - Objective measure of client AI adoption beyond self-reported surveys - Framework for segmenting clients by true AI integration maturity - Evidence that AI investment intensity correlates with business growth - Validation that measurement approach fundamentally shapes skills gap conclusions

docs.title: Revelio Labs
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-07-03

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Revelio Labs is a workforce intelligence platform that aggregates data from online professional profiles to construct longitudinal employment histories. By analyzing millions of publicly available career records, Revelio provides granular insights into workforce composition, movement, and evolution across industries and occupations.

docs.title: Data Collection Methodology
docs.text:
• Source Data: Publicly available online professional profiles (LinkedIn, company sites, etc.)
  • Aggregation: Constructs longitudinal employment histories for individual workers
  • Fields Captured: Employers, job titles, employment dates, locations, seniority levels
  • Weighting: Adjusts for differential platform usage to improve labor market representativeness

docs.title: Seniority Classification System
docs.text: Revelio's seven-point seniority field enables precise workforce segmentation: - Entry-Level: Seniority 1-2 (typically 0-3 years experience) - Non-Entry: Seniority 3-7 - Manager-Plus: Seniority 4-7 - Engineering Roles: Further segmented by technical specialization

docs.title: Key Applications in AI Research
docs.text: Revelio data enabled the Ramp-Revelio 2026 study to: - Track monthly employment changes at 21,559 firms - Analyze role-specific impacts of AI adoption - Measure entry-level vs. senior workforce composition shifts - Validate findings against traditional labor statistics through RPLS

docs.title: Validation and Reliability
docs.text:
• Revelio Public Labor Statistics (RPLS): Benchmarked against official statistics
  • Weighting Methodology: Corrects for platform usage differences across demographics
  • Academic Adoption: Used in numerous peer-reviewed studies on workforce dynamics
  • Limitations: Coverage varies by occupation, industry, and geography

docs.title: Key Findings Enabled by Revelio Data
docs.text:
• High-intensity AI adopters increase entry-level headcount by 12.0%
  • Employment gains are broad across roles (engineering, sales, admin, customer service)
  • Sectoral differences in AI impact are concentrated in Information firms
  • Pre-adoption growth trajectories differ significantly between adopters and non-adopters

docs.title: Relevance to Market Research
docs.text: Revelio's approach offers market researchers: - Granular workforce composition data beyond traditional surveys - Longitudinal tracking of career progression and role evolution - Objective measurement of talent market dynamics - Framework for analyzing how AI reshapes specific job functions

docs.title: Related Research

  • Complements PwC's occupational exposure analysis with firm-level workforce insights
  • Provides empirical foundation for the value-chain-shift concept in research organizations

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This chart compares AI adoption rates across different measurement methodologies. The Ramp/Revelio series tracks paid-AI adoption in their analytical panel, showing adoption rates rising from approximately 10% in early 2023 to over 60% by mid-2026. This is contrasted with U.S. Census estimates (17-20%), Atlanta Fed Survey of Business Uncertainty (78%), and Yotzov et al. executive survey estimates (69%). The visualization demonstrates that "AI adoption" lacks a single empirical rate due to varying measurement approaches - some capture broad organizational use while others measure only paid, sustained adoption with payment traces.

docs.title: Key Insights
docs.text:
• Different methodologies yield dramatically different adoption rates (from 17% to 78%)
  • Ramp/Revelio measures sustained paid adoption requiring $100/month for 3 consecutive months
  • Executive surveys capture broader organizational awareness but may overstate actual implementation

docs.title: AI Spend Per Employee Methodology
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-07-03

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A direct measurement approach for quantifying firm-level AI adoption intensity by calculating monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after adoption begins. Developed by Ramp economists for the 2026 AI Jobs Impact Study, this methodology addresses limitations of occupational exposure scores and survey-based adoption measures.

docs.title: Calculation
docs.text:
PEPM_i = (Σ from m=0 to 2 of AI_{i,G_i+m}) / (3 × HC_{i,G_i-1})

Where: - AI_{it} = monthly AI vendor spend - G_i = first month of sustained AI adoption - HC_{i,G_i-1} = baseline headcount in month before adoption

docs.title: Implementation Steps
docs.text:
1. Adoption Definition: First month of earliest three-consecutive-month spell with ≥$100 AI spend monthly
  2. Intensity Measurement: Calculate PEPM using first three post-adoption months
  3. Group Classification: Low intensity = bottom two PEPM terciles, High intensity = top tercile
  4. Comparison Design: Compare earlier adopters to later adopters in same intensity group

docs.text: Method Limitations PEPM Advantages Occupational exposure scores Vary only across occupations, not firms Measures actual firm adoption decisions Executive surveys Capture awareness not implementation Tracks payment data showing actual usage AI-related job postings Proxy for interest not adoption Measures direct financial commitment Resume AI skills Lagging indicator of adoption Captures immediate spending behavior

docs.title: Epoch score
docs.text: The EPOCH score measures the reliance on human capabilities in various occupations.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The EPOCH score, pwc's proprietary metric, quantifies occupational reliance on human capabilities difficult for AI to replicate. Ranging 0-1, it evaluates dimensions including empathy, creativity, physical dexterity, and face-to-face interaction through job description analysis and expert assessment. Figure 10 of the 2026 report provides definitive validation: new tasks added to AI-exposed roles since 2022 show EPOCH scores 2.5 times higher in the top exposure quartile (0.47) versus bottom quartile (0.19), proving AI shifts work toward human-intensive activities. Figure 11 further demonstrates its significance by showing democratised roles (0.48) and professionalised roles (0.45) maintain substantially higher scores than low exposure roles (0.26), indicating both AI impact pathways increase human reliance. The methodology explains key economic trends: occupations with higher EPOCH scores in AI-exposed roles command greater wage premiums (Figure 15), as human skills become scarcer value drivers. Crucially, the score helps operationalize the ai-job-future-framework's 'AI's limitations' dimension by identifying tasks requiring human oversight. The report shows EPOCH scores are rising fastest in high-exposure roles (Figure 9), with the top quartile's score increasing 116% from 2023-2025. This metric has become essential for organizations mapping future skill requirements, particularly in designing professionalised-jobs and addressing the human elements of 'superstar' company success (Figure 12). Policymakers also use it to target workforce development initiatives where human capabilities provide sustainable competitive advantages.

docs.title: Pwc ai occupational exposure index
docs.text: PwC's proprietary methodology to measure the degree to which different occupations are exposed to AI capabilities.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: PwC's AI Occupational Exposure Index quantifies occupational susceptibility to AI through a multi-dimensional methodology. Ranging 0-1, it analyzes 2,000+ work activities across 800+ occupations, assessing technical feasibility, economic viability, and adoption timelines for AI automation. The 2026 report reveals 74% of jobs have meaningful exposure (quartiles 2-4), with the top quartile experiencing transformative impacts. Figure 3 demonstrates how the index interacts with expertise requirements, showing high-exposure jobs either increase (professionalisation) or decrease (democratization) expertise demands. The methodology underpins critical findings: Figure 7 uses it to segment entry-level job trends, Figure 9 to analyze skill change velocity (top quartile changing 2.2x faster), and Figure 12 to correlate exposure with productivity. Notably, the index evolved to incorporate generative AI capabilities post-2022, explaining accelerated impacts observed after ChatGPT's release. Organizations apply it to identify at-risk roles, prioritize reskilling, and benchmark against industry peers—particularly valuable for navigating the 'superstar effect' where top-quartile firms achieve 163% productivity growth. The report details sector-specific adaptations (e.g., healthcare's focus on diagnostic support roles), making it versatile for workforce planning. When combined with the epoch-score, the index forms the empirical foundation of the ai-job-future-framework, enabling organizations to systematically address all four framework questions. Its longitudinal design (2012-2025 data) provides unprecedented insight into AI's accelerating labor market transformation.

docs.title: Ai specialist roles
docs.text: Job roles specifically focused on the development, implementation, and maintenance of AI systems, growing eight times faster than total job postings.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: AI specialist roles are experiencing explosive growth, expanding eight times faster than total job postings according to Figure 16 of the PwC 2026 report. From a 2012 baseline of zero, these roles reached 11.0x growth by 2025 versus 2.0x for total postings, with acceleration intensifying post-2022. Figure 16b shows pervasive sector adoption: Technology, Media and Telecoms leads at 11.4% of sector roles, followed by Health Industries (4.0%), Financial Services (3.0%), and Manufacturing (2.0%). Core responsibilities include AI system architecture, prompt engineering, ethical governance, and domain-specific integration—often blending technical and business skills. Figure 15 confirms these roles command significant wage premiums averaging 62%, with Consumer Markets reaching 118%. The report identifies three growth drivers: urgent demand for AI implementation expertise, the need to address [[ai's limitations]] in quality control and edge cases, and regulatory compliance requirements. Crucially, Figure 12 links this growth to the 'superstar effect', as top-performing AI-exposed companies achieve 163% productivity growth by strategically deploying these specialists. Unlike traditional tech roles, modern AI specialists increasingly operate in hybrid functions (e.g., AI-augmented [[pharmacists]] or [[financial-analysts]]), requiring both domain knowledge and technical proficiency. This trend positions AI specialization as a critical career pathway across the economy, with implications for education systems needing to develop curricula aligned with the ai-job-future-framework.

docs.title: Democratised jobs
docs.text: Democratised jobs are occupations reshaped by AI to demand less human expertise, representing 52% of advertised positions globally.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: Democratised jobs—where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans—constitute 52% of global postings but show distinct market patterns. Figure 2 illustrates this through roles like [[inventory-clerks]] (AI automates inventory management but humans move stock) and [[recruiters]] (AI screens CVs but humans negotiate contracts). While numerous, Figure 4 shows they've added skills at half the pace of professionalised roles (33% vs 68% growth 2018-2025), and Figure 5 confirms slower salary growth (26% vs 37% since 2021). However, Figure 11 reveals a critical nuance: democratised roles maintain the highest average epoch-score (0.48), indicating continued reliance on human capabilities for remaining tasks—often involving physical dexterity, adaptability in unstructured environments, or interpersonal interactions. This explains why these roles remain resilient despite reduced expertise requirements. The report warns that while democratisation expands job accessibility (e.g., enabling non-experts to perform complex analysis via AI tools), it may compress career ladders without structured progression paths. Figure 9 contextualizes this within skills transformation, showing democratised roles still experience 2.2x faster skill changes than low-exposure jobs. Organizations can leverage this trend through the ai-job-future-framework's 'Environmental forces' dimension, designing roles that combine AI efficiency with uniquely human execution—particularly valuable in sectors like retail and logistics where physical interaction remains essential.

docs.title: AI Deskilling and Core Human Capacities
docs.text: Recent research reveals that AI adoption poses specific risks to human-intensive skills through what Ferdman (2026) terms "capacity impoverishment." Unlike skill obsolescence in domains like hunting or basket-weaving, the deskilling of core human capacities diminishes us as humans and undermines our flourishing.

docs.title: Core Capacities at Risk
docs.text:
The following capacities are particularly vulnerable to AI-mediated deskilling:

  • Epistemic capacities: Theoretical rationality (thinking, considering reasons, forming beliefs) and practical rationality (phronesis or wisdom)
  • Social capacities: Moral capacity and abilities for developing meaningful relationships
  • Creative capacity: Making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas
  • Volitional capacity: The ability to exert effort, overcome difficulty, and persevere

These capacities differ from technical skills because they are constitutive of human flourishing. As Ferdman explains, "the deskilling of our core human capacities is bad because inadequate development of these capacities can lead to 'capacity impoverishment,' which, in turn, diminishes us as humans."

docs.title: Structural Dimensions of Deskilling
docs.text:
Deskilling is not merely an individual responsibility issue. AI creates systemic conditions that inhibit capacity development through:

  • Capacity-hostile environments: That restrict action possibilities for capacity cultivation
  • Undermined habituation: Short-circuiting the gradual process of skill development
  • Reduced intersubjectivity: Diminishing opportunities for shared valuing of capacities
  • Disembodiment: Limiting physical presence necessary for certain capacities

For market research professionals, this means AI tools that automate data interpretation without preserving opportunities for researchers to develop critical thinking may ultimately undermine the quality of insights produced.

docs.title: Evidence of Deskilling
docs.text:
Studies show AI dependence leads to: - Erosion of critical thinking (Bonicalzi et al. 2023) - Decline in decision-making and analytical reasoning (Zhai et al. 2024) - Reduced activity awareness and competence maintenance (Rinta-Kahila et al. 2023)

See capacity-hostile-environments and ai-deskilling-structural-problem for related frameworks analyzing how AI affects human capacities.

Figure 8 reveals that in the US top AI exposure quartile, entry-level positions requiring traditionally senior skills (strategic decision-making, complex problem-solving, leadership) are projected to grow 35% between 2019-2025, while non-seniorised roles decline by 10%. This phenomenon occurs because AI tools automate foundational tasks previously performed by junior staff—such as data entry for [[inventory-clerks]] or CV screening for [[recruiters]] (Figure 2)—effectively compressing career ladders. Consequently, new graduates must now demonstrate competencies typically associated with 3-5 years of experience. Key senior skills appearing in entry-level descriptions include advanced data interpretation, cross-functional collaboration, and client relationship management, particularly in high-growth professionalised-jobs like environmental engineering. Figure 7 contextualizes this within broader market trends, showing high AI exposure quartile entry-level postings have flatlined since 2022, suggesting seniorisation may be a prerequisite for growth in AI-impacted roles. The report warns this trend could exacerbate early-career inequality without structured mentorship programs, while creating opportunities for accelerated career progression in organizations embracing the ai-job-future-framework.

docs.title: Burning Glass Institute: Beyond the Binary
Overview
docs.text: Published in January 2026 by the [[burning-glass-institute]], "Beyond the Binary" represents a landmark analysis challenging the conventional wisdom that AI will either automate or augment jobs. Instead, the research demonstrates that automation and augmentation are frequently occurring simultaneously within the same occupations.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: The study analyzed labor-market data from millions of job postings across 759 occupations, developing metrics to measure both automation exposure (tasks AI can perform) and augmentation exposure (tasks where AI enhances human capabilities).

docs.title: Correlation of Automation and Augmentation
docs.text:
• Exposure to automation and augmentation is strongly positively correlated across occupations
  • Jobs most exposed to automation are also highly exposed to augmentation
  • This finding validates the "automation-augmentation paradox" first identified by Raisch & Krakowski (2021)

docs.title: Skill Demand Shifts
docs.text:
• Automation-exposed skills were 16% more likely to see demand decline compared to baseline skills
  • Augmentation-exposed skills were 7% more likely to see demand increase
  • This creates a net shift in the composition of work rather than simple job elimination

docs.title: The Entry-Level Challenge
docs.text: The report identifies a critical concern: junior workers traditionally built expertise through foundational tasks (drafting reports, conducting research, building models) that AI can now perform or accelerate. This threatens established apprenticeship models and expertise development pathways.

docs.title: Real-World Examples
docs.text:
• Project managers see routine scheduling automated while strategic coordination becomes more valuable
  • Analysts spend less time producing first-pass models but more time interpreting and communicating implications
  • Consultants can produce drafts instantly but face higher premium on the quality of underlying thinking

docs.title: Implications
docs.text: The study concludes that AI is not neatly dividing the labor market but is changing the composition of work inside jobs. Organizations risk "automating the developmental tasks before they have redesigned the learning pathway," potentially gaining short-term efficiency while weakening their future talent base.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Market Research Institute International (MRII) 2026 global study represents the fourth annual comprehensive analysis of market research and insights professionals worldwide. Conducted by [[ed-keller]] and released at IIEX North America in May 2026, this research surveyed professionals across multiple regions to understand industry sentiment, AI adoption patterns, and evolving skill requirements in the insights sector.

docs.title: Professional Optimism vs. AI Readiness
docs.text:
• 58% of insights professionals believe their function will become more important in the future, demonstrating strong conviction in the field's relevance despite AI disruption
  • More than half report high levels of job satisfaction and expect the coming year to be better than the previous
  • This optimism exists alongside significant readiness challenges, creating what researchers describe as "the defining story of the insights industry today"

docs.title: AI Adoption Patterns
docs.text:
• Nearly 8 in 10 professionals report favorable views of generative AI
  • Approximately 50% use AI regularly in some capacity
  • Only 1 in 10 report AI is fully embedded in day-to-day workflows
  • Across 15 potential use cases (questionnaire design, data analysis, reporting), no single application has emerged as a dominant "killer app" (top adoption at ~40%)

docs.title: Skills Gap Analysis
docs.text:
The study identified a critical disconnect between: - Skills professionals want to develop: AI/digital skills, advanced analytics, technical capabilities - Skills leaders value most: business acumen, communication, ability to influence decisions, connecting insights to outcomes

This gap has significant consequences, as opportunities for learning and growth are among the biggest drivers of job satisfaction and retention.

docs.title: Value Chain Shift
docs.text:
As articulated by [[pam-forbus]] of Mondelez: "AI will increasingly answer questions, deliver insights, execute projects, and support stakeholders faster and at lower cost than ever before. That doesn't diminish the role of insights teams; it fundamentally changes it."

The study concludes that value is moving upstream - insights teams must evolve to shape decisions, drive growth, build AI-leveraging systems, and influence strategy rather than merely delivering answers.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: The study surveyed global market research professionals through structured questionnaires and follow-up interviews, with particular attention to AI exposure metrics and skill development priorities. It represents one of the most comprehensive longitudinal analyses of AI's impact on the insights industry.
